messages.author: 25d2ffb7b5f86e67
messages.subject: sampling question
parts:
Hello everyone,
I am sampling urban birds in residential areas. Line transects are limited =
to public streets. The habitat is stratified in narrow bands. Typically, a =
four-lane street has two traffic lanes in the center and a parking lane at =
each curbside. Next is a narrow pedestrian lane on either side. In some cou=
ntries residential lots are enclosed by high walls along their perimeter, w=
hich restrict visual detection. In the USA custom and regulations tend to p=
rohibit such walls so that there is a band of front yards, usually with gra=
ss lawns and good visibility, then a row of houses, and finally a row of re=
ar yards, typically enclosed with high privacy fences.=A0Birds perching on =
the proximal side of roofs can be detected but those on the distal side can=
not. Birds in the rear yards are frequently heard but seldom seen.
=A0
In older neighborhoods a line of utility poles is usually situated between =
the street and pedestrian walk along one side of the street. These poles ha=
ve multiple layers of wires; a ground wire at the top, 2 or more electric l=
ines below that, and various telephone and TV cable lines lower down. These=
multiple wires provide favorite perches for birds. Trees may be present al=
ong one or both sides of the street, but heavily pruned adjacent to the wir=
es. Birds perched on the wires are numerous and conspicuous and detection i=
s close to 1. Birds in tree canopies have detection less than one.
=A0
While traversing the street centerline would preserve habitat symmetry, saf=
ety reasons preclude this. The observer can choose to walk beneath the util=
ity lines and produce heaping in the 0 to 3 meter range, or walk on the opp=
osite side of the street and produce heaping in the 8 to 12 meter range. Ar=
e there any theoretical reasons why an observer should choose one side of t=
he street or the other?
=A0
Robert W. McFarlane
Houston, Texas, USA

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: sampling question
parts:
Robert,

When one does not walk randomly located transect lines, then a critical
assumption of standard distance sampling is violated: that the true
distribution of animals with respect to distance is known. Therefore
any change in frequency of detections with distance for a line transect
cannot be interpreted as indicating change in detectability - it could
be that or it could be change in density. In other words, standard
distance sampling methods do not apply. Tiago Marques devoted much of
his PhD thesis to an examination of these issues, and (somewhat complex)
methods for trying to get around them - I recommend you have a look at
it. A copy is at http://hdl.handle.net/10023/391 See also the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book section 7.8.5.

It seems to me that you could consider
(a) a strip transect of out to a distance where every animal of the
target species is detectable. This will only give you density in this
strip however, and not density in the town.
(b) a separate study to get at detectability (for example where you have
people visually tracking animals to set up "trials" for the line
transect observer and then doing logistic regression to get the
detection function), so that you can then estimate the density gradient.
There may be something about this in Tiago's thesis.

As for your specific question about where to walk: I think you have far
bigger concerns to address, as outlined above!

All the best,

- Len
